entry.title: Claude Code skill
entry.content:
Install the tik skill so Claude drives a store correctly — recording evidence and letting stages derive, instead of setting statuses.

Install the tik skill into Claude Code and Claude gains working knowledge of tik: it recognises a store, records facts with tik set rather than inventing a status field, reads tik explain before asking a person anything, and authors process definitions whose stages derive from evidence instead of listing activities.

That last part is the reason the skill exists. The failure mode for any model writing a tik process is a task list wearing a process costume — stages named after activities, with nothing following from anything. The skill carries the design law that rules it out, along with the closed guard vocabulary and the authoring loop that checks the result.

The skill lives in this repository under skills/tik/, packaged as a Claude Code plugin by the manifests in .claude-plugin/.

Install

Add this repository as a plugin marketplace, then install the plugin:

/plugin marketplace add metio/tik
/plugin install tik@tik

Claude activates the skill whenever a repository holds a tickets/ or .tik/ directory, an actors registry, or processes/*.edn — or when you mention tik, tickets, processes, or stages.

From the MCP server

A tik MCP server also serves the skill, through the MCP Skills extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills). With the server registered, Claude Code v2.1.331 or later lists the skill as <server>:tik, for example tik:tik, and loads the copy built into that server, so it matches the server’s version without a plugin install. Claude Code lists MCP skills only over MCP revision 2026-07-28, which tik mcp and tik serve speak. See MCP server for how the manifest is signed and checked.

What it grants Claude

The skill teaches the CLI surface and the model behind it:

  • The daily loop — tik ls, tik next, tik new, tik set, tik explain, tik status, and the selector grammar for filtering a board.
  • Corrections — retract, dispute, and the fact that a dispute is answered only by a different value, so Claude does not try to clear one by retyping the same fact.
  • Authoring — tik author, the guard vocabulary, and the lint, simulate, and test loop that proves a definition before a real ticket depends on it.
  • The one design law — a stage is defined by what must be TRUE to reach it, never by who moved what.

It also knows when not to act: an unreachable step in explain means waiting is pointless and the definition or the role register needs fixing, not patience.

Hearing about changes

tik notify runs a local notifier that re-derives and verifies every ticket whose log changed and pushes a hint of each stage change to the sessions that asked for it, over a Unix socket only your user can reach:

tik notify --config ~/.config/tik/notify.edn

{:stores {"metio" "~/git/github.com/metio/.tik"}
 :window "PT5S"
 :sinks [{:store "metio" :where "stage=:asked"
          :command ["notify-send" "tik" "{line}"]}]}

A Claude Code session subscribes by running tik notify watch under the Monitor tool, which feeds each output line back to Claude:

tik notify watch --store metio --where "fact:request.from=infra.run"

Each line is one JSON hint naming the store, the ticket, its title, the stages it left and entered, and the actor of the event that moved it. A hint holds no fact values and is never evidence: Claude re-derives with tik status before acting on it. tik notify channel delivers the same hints as a Claude Code channel to a session started with --dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>. The channel speaks only the legacy initialize handshake and answers server/discover with -32601. It reads at most 1 MiB per stdin line, like tik mcp: a longer line, or one that is not valid JSON, answers a parse error (-32700) whose data.rule names the rule, and the next line is read. Hints sent while nobody was subscribed are not replayed, so keep a slow fallback poll. The decisions behind this are in ADR 0040 .

For agents generally

The skill is one surface over a derivation every tool can read. The gated agent commands enforce the same boundary without any prompt-side cooperation:

tik agent actions 3184 --actor bot
tik agent set 3184 severity=:high --actor bot

An agent sees only what the frontier admits for its role, and anything else is refused with the derived reason. Because the boundary is the derivation rather than an instruction, it cannot be talked around.

This site also publishes /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt, so a model can read the documentation directly.

entry.title: Clojure library
entry.content:
Read, verify and derive one ticket of a store in process with tik.api, read-only and without starting a process.

tik.api gives a JVM, babashka or native-image program the answers of tik status and tik verify for one ticket without running the CLI. It never writes to the store, signs, runs a probe, touches the network or starts a process.

(require '[tik.api :as api])

(def store (api/open-store "/path/to/.tik"))   ; the dir holding tickets/ or tik.db

(api/derive store "f106aa78")
;; => {:ticket #uuid "f106aa78-…" :title "…"
;;     :rules {:process :skilled-change :version 2 :hash "sha256-…"}
;;     :current [:scoped] :reached [:scoped]
;;     :facts {[:kind] {:status :present :value :feat :by "claude"} …}
;;     :missing-parents nil
;;     :definition {:pinned "sha256-…" :derived-under "sha256-…" :source :archive}
;;     :at #inst "…"}

(:ok? (api/verify-ticket store "f106aa78"))

Add tik as a git dependency in deps.edn:

{:deps {io.github.metio/tik {:git/sha "<commit>"}}}

The calls

  • (open-store root) or (open-store root {:limits {…}}) opens the store whose root is root, the directory holding tickets/ (file store) or tik.db (SQLite store). Nothing is discovered from parent directories.
  • (resolve-id store ref) takes a uuid, the full id, or a prefix of at least 8 characters naming exactly one ticket.
  • (ticket store ref) returns the ticket’s events in reduction order.
  • (derive store ref {:at instant}) returns the ticket’s title, rules, current and reached stages and facts. They equal what tik status <id> --edn --at <instant> prints. When the definition found in the store does not hash to the ticket’s pin, derive refuses unless {:allow-unpinned-definition true} is passed.
  • (verify-ticket store ref) runs the tik verify ladder for that ticket with the same code as the CLI and returns it as data: :ok?, :failures, one summary per event (:integrity and :signature, which is :verified, :delegated, :unsigned, :unchecked or :failed) and every check as an item.

tik.api/version is the contract’s version; it changes only when a documented key, argument or refusal changes meaning or goes away.

Refusals

Every refusal is an ex-info whose :type is in the tik.api namespace: not-a-store, ambiguous-store, backend-unavailable, invalid-argument, invalid-id, unknown-ticket, ambiguous-id (with :candidates), too-large (with :limit and :actual), unreadable, definition-missing, definition-mismatch, malformed-roles, underivable and read-only.

Differences from the CLI

  • Signatures are verified in process (Ed25519, Ed25519 security keys, ML-DSA-65). A key type only ssh-keygen reads is :unchecked, and its check fails where tik verify would ask ssh-keygen.
  • Every event, sidecar and config file is measured before it is read, and a symbolic link inside a ticket directory is refused. The defaults are tik.api/default-limits.
  • A SQLite store is opened read-only and needs the SQLite driver, which babashka lacks. A native image that reads SQLite stores or identity bindings must require tik.store.sqlite-jdbc or cheshire.core at build time.

The reasoning is recorded in ADR 0044 .

entry.title: GitHub Actions
entry.content:
Failed workflow runs as ci-failure tickets, one per failure streak.
tik bridge github --config github.edn             # poll once
tik bridge github --config github.edn --webhook   # serve workflow_run deliveries

tik bridge github turns failed GitHub Actions runs into tickets under the ci-failure process. One ticket covers one failure streak: the consecutive failed runs of one workflow on one branch, from the first failure after a green run up to the next green run. Further failures attach to the open ticket as ci/run/<id>/<attempt> artifacts, the next green run is recorded as forge.green-run, and a failure after that opens a new ticket. Cancelled, skipped and neutral runs neither extend nor end a streak. GitLab pipelines feed the same process with the same facts, so the metrics below cover both forges.

Configuration

{:repos   ["metio/tik" {:repo "metio/jaas" :branches ["main" "next"]}]
 :orgs    ["metio" "sebhoss"]       ; every non-archived repository, default branch
 :exclude ["metio/scratch"]
 :token   {:env "GITHUB_TOKEN"}     ; or {:command …} / {:file …} / {:credential …}
 :tokens  {"sebhoss" {:command ["pass" "show" "github/sebhoss"]}}
 :api     "https://api.github.com"  ; a GitHub Enterprise Server URL also works
 :actor   "github"
 :actions {:process   :ci-failure
           :lookback  "P14D"        ; streaks with no run newer than this are left alone
           :max-pages 5             ; history pages fetched to find a streak's first run
           :failing   #{"failure" "timed_out" "startup_failure"}
           :green     #{"success"}}
 :webhook {:secret {:env "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"} :port 8787}}

Each source is enabled by its block; :actions is the only source so far. A token needs read access to Actions and metadata on the repositories it covers. :tokens maps a repository owner to its own token, because a fine-grained GitHub token is scoped to one resource owner; owners without an entry use :token, then $GITHUB_TOKEN. An :orgs entry may also name a user account: its public repositories are listed, plus its private ones when that owner’s token belongs to the user. A failure listing one owner is reported and skips that owner only.

The bridge actor (github by default) must be registered in actors with the key in TIK_KEY. The ci-failure process’s :bridge role holds only the forge bridges (github, gitlab), so nobody else can open or recover a streak.

Each ticket records forge.host, forge.repo, forge.owner, forge.workflow, forge.branch, forge.first-run and forge.head-sha, plus repo, the repository’s name as a keyword (:tik): the value tik new records for a ticket made inside the checkout. A store above many checkouts therefore shows a repository’s CI failures next to its other tickets (tik ls --all --where 'fact:repo=:tik').

Polling and webhooks

Both drivers run the same sync and are idempotent, so they can run side by side and on several replicas. A ticket id hashes the repository id, workflow, branch and first failed run. A ticket is dated by the creation time of its first failed run, and each later event by the start time of the run attempt it records. GitHub never changes either timestamp, whereas it does rewrite updated_at on old runs. Two replicas syncing the same history therefore write identical events, and a re-poll writes nothing. Time to :recovered runs from the first failed run’s creation to the start of the green run.

Run both from tik backend (pipelines.edn):

{:pipelines
 [{:id :github-poll    :every "PT10M" :run ["bridge" "github"] :as "github"}
  {:id :github-webhook :watch true    :run ["bridge" "github" "--webhook"] :as "github"}]}

For the webhook, point a repository or organization webhook at the listener with content type application/json, the shared secret, and the Workflow runs event. Deliveries without a valid X-Hub-Signature-256 are refused with 401. A delivery only names the workflow; the bridge then reads that workflow’s history from the API, so a lost delivery is repaired by the next poll.

A streak whose first run lies beyond :max-pages of history is skipped with a message instead of being opened on a guessed start, because a guessed start would give replicas different ticket ids.

Triage

The cause is the one fact the forge cannot supply:

tik set <id> cause=dependency   # flaky | code | dependency | config | infra | upstream

A ticket reaches :resolved once it has both a cause and a bridge-signed green run.

Metrics

tik stats groups any tickets by a fact and derives the counts and the time from creation to a stage:

tik stats --by forge.repo --split cause --until :resolved --where 'fact:forge.workflow'
tik stats --by forge.host --until :recovered
tik stats --by forge.repo --format json

The columns are the ticket count, how many have not reached the stage, and the median, 90th-percentile and mean time to reach it. The fact:forge.workflow term restricts the count to CI-failure tickets. Every number is recomputed from the ticket logs on each run.

entry.title: GitLab pipelines
entry.content:
Failed GitLab pipelines as ci-failure tickets, one per failure streak, optionally through an SSH port forward.
tik bridge gitlab --config gitlab.edn   # poll once

tik bridge gitlab turns failed GitLab pipelines into ci-failure tickets, with the same streak rules, facts and metrics as GitHub Actions . A pipeline has no workflow id; its source (push, schedule, web, …) takes that place, so a failing nightly schedule and green push pipelines on the same branch are separate streaks, titled push pipeline, schedule pipeline and so on. Pipelines with any status other than failed and success (canceled, skipped, manual) neither extend nor end a streak.

Configuration

{:url        "https://gitlab.example"   ; the web URL; the API is <url>/api/v4
 :membership true                       ; every project the token's account is a member of
 :groups     ["team/platform"]          ; every project of a group and its subgroups
 :projects   ["team/app" {:project "team/lib" :branches ["main" "next"]}]
 :exclude    ["team/platform/scratch"]
 :token      {:env "GITLAB_TOKEN"}      ; or {:command …} / {:file …} / {:credential …}
 :tunnel     {:ssh "admin@gitlab.example" :target "127.0.0.1:8080"}
 :actor      "gitlab"
 :pipelines  {:process   :ci-failure
              :lookback  "P14D"
              :max-pages 5
              :failing   #{"failed"}
              :green     #{"success"}}}

The token needs read access to the API (read_api). Archived projects are left out, and a project without :branches watches its default branch. A failure listing one group or project is reported and skips it only.

SSH port forward

Some GitLab instances only serve their API on the host itself. With :tunnel, the bridge runs ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:<free port>:<target> <ssh> for the duration of the sweep and sends the API requests to the local end. The forwarded target speaks plain HTTP; the connection that leaves the machine is the SSH one. Outside a tunnel, the bridge refuses a non-HTTPS API URL. The SSH destination must be an account allowed to forward ports, and ssh runs with BatchMode=yes, so its key must be usable without a prompt (an agent or an unencrypted key).

Retried pipelines

A retried pipeline keeps its id and shows only its latest outcome, so the bridge checks every green pipeline for a ticket opened on it and records the recovery there. GitLab’s pipeline list carries no start time, so such a recovery is dated by the pipeline’s creation and its time to :recovered reads as zero.

entry.title: Local service
entry.content:
Run the board, MCP, the bridges, backend and notify from the native binary, under systemd or by hand.

The native binary runs everything a long-running local install needs: tik serve for the board and MCP, tik bridge <kind> sweeps, tik backend for scheduled pipelines and tik notify for hints. It needs no JVM, no babashka and no checkout. Every release checks this with dev/native-smoke.sh, which drives the built binary through each of these against loopback stand-ins for GitHub, GitLab, Redmine, Odoo and an IMAP mailbox.

The environment

Variable Read by Meaning
TIK_ROOT every verb The store. Without it, tik uses the nearest ancestor holding .tik/, tickets/ or tik.db.
TIK_ACTOR every write The actor events are signed as. --actor overrides it.
TIK_KEY every write The ed25519 private key that signs. --key overrides it.
GITHUB_TOKEN bridge github The token when github.edn names neither :token nor :tokens.
GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET bridge github --webhook The HMAC secret when github.edn has no :webhook {:secret …}.
GITLAB_TOKEN bridge gitlab The token when gitlab.edn has no :token.
REDMINE_API_KEY bridge redmine The key when redmine.edn has no :key.
ODOO_PASSWORD bridge odoo The password when odoo.edn has no :password.
CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY any {:credential …} Set by systemd for LoadCredential=.
XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, XDG_STATE_HOME notify The default socket directory and the cursor.

Any secret in a bridge config can be a spec instead of a literal: {:command "pass show github"} (the first line of the command’s output), {:file "/run/secrets/x"}, {:env "NAME"} or {:credential "NAME"}. The credential form is the one to prefer under systemd: the secret never sits in a file you commit, in the environment or in argv. An unset variable, a missing file, a failing command and an empty or blank value are refused rather than read as an empty secret. A command has one minute to answer, its error output goes to tik’s stderr instead of into the refusal, and a file, credential or output longer than 64 KiB is refused.

The board and MCP

openssl rand -hex 32 > ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token
TIK_ROOT=~/work/.tik TIK_ACTOR=claude TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/claude_ed25519 \
  tik serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7777 \
    --mcp-token-file ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token --surfaces http,mcp

/ is the board, /tickets.edn and /explain/<id>.edn its data, and /mcp the MCP endpoint. Clients send the token as Authorization: Bearer <token>. /mcp answers both the initialize handshake and stateless 2026-07-28 requests; see MCP server . Calls on /mcp write as TIK_ACTOR, which is why the token is required and why serve listens on 127.0.0.1 unless --host says otherwise.

The bridges

Each sync bridge reads its config from the store root (github.edn, gitlab.edn, redmine.edn, odoo.edn, imap.edn), or from --config, sweeps once and exits 0, or 1 when any unit of the sweep failed:

export TIK_ROOT=~/work/.tik TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/github_ed25519
tik bridge github                       # github.edn: :token or GITHUB_TOKEN
tik bridge gitlab                       # gitlab.edn: :token or GITLAB_TOKEN
tik bridge redmine                      # redmine.edn: :key or REDMINE_API_KEY
tik bridge odoo                         # odoo.edn: :password or ODOO_PASSWORD
tik bridge imap                         # imap.edn: {:imap {:host … :user … :password …}}

The actor of a sweep is the config’s :actor (or github, gitlab, redmine, odoo), so TIK_KEY must be that actor’s key. A server that cannot be reached, or whose certificate does not chain to a CA the binary trusts, fails the sweep with a line naming the API, the address and the cause, and nothing is written. For a server behind a private CA, name a trust store holding that CA; the binary reads -D system properties before its verb:

tik -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=/etc/pki/internal.p12 \
    -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit bridge odoo

The detail of each bridge is on its own page: GitHub Actions , GitLab pipelines , Redmine and Odoo .

Under systemd

A timer per bridge, with the signing key and the remote’s secret handed over as credentials. The key file is readable only by the unit while it runs:

# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik-bridge@.service
[Unit]
Description=Sweep the %i tik bridge
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
EnvironmentFile=%h/.config/tik/bridge-%i.env
LoadCredential=tik-key:%h/.config/tik/%i_ed25519
Environment=TIK_KEY=%d/tik-key
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/tik bridge ${TIK_BRIDGE}

# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik-bridge@.timer
[Unit]
Description=Sweep the %i tik bridge every 10 minutes

[Timer]
OnBootSec=2min
OnUnitActiveSec=10min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# ~/.config/tik/bridge-github-work.env
TIK_BRIDGE=github
TIK_ROOT=/home/me/work/.tik

%d is the unit’s credentials directory. A secret the config fetches with {:credential "github-token"} arrives the same way, through another LoadCredential=github-token:<file> line. Enable one instance per bridge with systemctl --user enable --now tik-bridge@github-work.timer.

The board runs as a plain service:

# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik.service
[Unit]
Description=tik board and MCP on 127.0.0.1:7777

[Service]
Environment=TIK_ROOT=%h/work/.tik TIK_ACTOR=claude
LoadCredential=tik-key:%h/.config/tik/claude_ed25519
LoadCredential=mcp-token:%h/.local/state/tik/mcp-token
Environment=TIK_KEY=%d/tik-key
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/tik serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7777 \
  --mcp-token-file %d/mcp-token --surfaces http,mcp
# tik exits with 143 on the SIGTERM of a stop, which is no failure.
SuccessExitStatus=143
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

Pipelines instead of timers

tik backend runs the same sweeps from one process on an interval. Each pipeline runs as the actor its :as names, passed as --actor, which takes precedence over a bridge config’s :actor. TIK_KEY is that actor’s key, so one backend process signs as one actor, and the bridge role of each process (roles.edn) has to include it. Put pipelines.edn at the store root:

{:pipelines
 [{:id :github  :every "PT10M" :as "tik-backend" :run ["bridge" "github"]}
  {:id :redmine :every "PT10M" :as "tik-backend" :run ["bridge" "redmine"]}
  {:id :board   :watch true                      :run ["serve" "--port" "7777"]}]}

TIK_ROOT=~/work/.tik TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/backend_ed25519 tik backend

A failing pipeline logs and the others carry on; a :watch pipeline is restarted with backoff when it exits.

Several stores in one backend

A config with :stores serves several stores from one process. Each store signs with its own key as its own actor, and its board and MCP answer below /s/<store>/ with that store’s own token:

;; ~/.config/tik/backend.edn
{:stores {:work {:root "~/work/.tik" :org "work" :actor "claude"
                 :key {:credential "tik-work-key"}
                 :mcp-token-file "~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token-work"}
          :home {:root "~/home/.tik" :org "home" :actor "claude"
                 :key {:command ["pass" "show" "tik/home"]}}}
 :serve {:host "127.0.0.1" :port 7777}
 :notify {}
 :pipelines [{:id :github-work :store :work :every "PT10M" :run ["bridge" "github"]}]}

tik backend --config ~/.config/tik/backend.edn
  • :key is a path, {:file …}, {:credential …} or {:command …}. A command’s whole output is written to an owner-only file below XDG_RUNTIME_DIR for as long as the backend runs. {:env …} is refused.
  • At start, each key must sign as the store’s :actor according to that store’s own actors file. Two stores with different :org may not resolve to the same key unless :allow-shared-keys [[:work :home]] says so.
  • An MCP token file must hold at least 32 characters and be readable by you only, and each store needs its own. A token sent to another store’s path is refused with 401.
  • A pipeline names its :store. It runs as that store’s actor, or as :as, which that store’s actors file must grant the key to. It may not pass --key, --actor or --config, and may not run serve, notify, mcp or backend, which the backend provides for every store itself.
  • :notify takes the settings of a notify.edn and watches every store of the backend.
  • TIK_ROOT, TIK_KEY, TIK_PQ_KEY and TIK_ACTOR must not be set in the backend’s environment, and neither may GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, GITLAB_TOKEN, REDMINE_API_KEY or ODOO_PASSWORD: every pipeline inherits the environment, so a token meant for one store’s bridge would reach all of them. Name the secret in the bridge’s config instead.

Any problem with any store refuses the whole backend and lists every problem, so a running backend always serves every store it names.

Bridges and mailboxes as pipelines

A multi-store backend replaces one systemd timer per bridge. Each run of a pipeline is a child process of the same binary that sees only its own store’s root, key and actor, so a bridge signs as its own delegate in its own store, and nothing one run keeps in memory reaches another store’s.

{:stores {...}
 :on-failure {:run ["notify-send" "--urgency=critical" "tik {store}/{pipeline}" "{reason}"]
              :repeat "PT1H"}
 :pipelines
 [{:id :github-work :store :work :every "PT10M" :as "github"
   :key {:credential "github-work-key"} :config "github.edn" :run ["bridge" "github"]}
  {:id :redmine-work :store :work :every "PT10M" :jitter "PT2M" :timeout "PT5M" :as "redmine"
   :key {:credential "redmine-work-key"} :run ["bridge" "redmine"]}
  {:id :support-mail :store :work :watch true :as "mail"
   :key {:credential "mail-work-key"} :config "imap.edn" :run ["bridge" "imap" "--watch"]}]}
Key Meaning Default
:every The interval of a scheduled pipeline, as an ISO-8601 duration. Fires sit on a grid from the backend’s start, so they do not drift by the run time.
:jitter Each fire lands at a random point within this window after its grid point. PT1M, at most half of :every
:timeout A run still going after this is stopped (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL five seconds later) and counts as failed. :every
:watch A continuous pipeline, restarted after 1 s, doubling to 60 s while it keeps failing fast, and back to 1 s once a run lasted a minute.
:config The verb’s config file, relative to the store’s root, absolute, or ~/…; it must exist when the backend starts. the verb’s default file at the store’s root
:as, :key The delegate the run signs as, and its key, which the store’s actors file must grant to it. the store’s actor and key

The backend’s own keys:

  • No overlap. A pipeline due while its previous run still goes is not started again; the skip is logged and the next fire is its next grid point. Different pipelines run at the same time.
  • Catch-up. Fires missed while the backend was stopped or the machine slept collapse into one run, which lands within the jitter window of the moment the backend noticed, at most 30 seconds after a resume.
  • :on-failure runs a command, without a shell, when a run fails or times out, with {store}, {pipeline}, {exit} and {reason} filled in. A pipeline is reported when it starts failing and again every :repeat while it keeps failing; "PT0S" reports every failure, as a unit’s OnFailure= does.
  • The journal. Every line is labelled [store/pipeline], and under systemd it carries a priority, so journalctl --user -u tik-backend -p warning shows the pipelines’ error output and the failure reports.
  • :exec names the command that runs this tik. The native binary and babashka find themselves; set it when neither applies.

Two pipelines of stores with different :org may not sign with the same key unless :allow-shared-keys names the pair of stores: one organisation’s delegate never signs for another’s.

Mailboxes

bridge imap reads one mailbox under :imap, or several under :mailboxes. Every other top-level key is a default for each mailbox, so adding a support address is one more list entry:

;; imap.edn at the store's root
{:dkim {:require true :authserv-id "mx.example.org"}
 :default-actor "mail"
 :mailboxes
 [{:id "support-example-org" :process :support
   :imap {:host "imap.example.org" :user "support@example.org"
          :password {:command ["pass" "show" "mail/support@example.org"]}}}
  {:id "support-app" :process :app-support
   :imap {:host "imap.example.org" :user "support@app.example"
          :password {:credential "support-app-imap"}}}]}

Each mailbox has its own connection, its own backoff and its own :process, and its lines are labelled with its :id. bridge imap --mailbox <id> reads only that one. A :mailboxes list, and every mailbox a backend watches, must:

  • require DKIM at a pinned verifier, :dkim {:require true :authserv-id …}, the id your receiving MX stamps on Authentication-Results, so a forged From is never credited to anybody (see below);
  • take its password from {:command …}, {:credential …} or {:file …}, never a literal and never {:env …};
  • under a backend, be signed by a key the store grants to every actor a mailbox records mail as: :default-actor and each :from->actor value.

The DKIM verdict

tik reads only the topmost Authentication-Results header of a message, the first one in its header block. The MTA that delivered the message prepended that header above every header the sender wrote, so a sender cannot place a header above it. When the topmost header names a verifier other than :authserv-id, the message is refused, even if a header further down claims the trusted id and dkim=pass. The From domain must then be the header.d of a dkim=pass in that header, or a subdomain of it.

This holds only when your receiving MTA stamps every message it delivers. A message it delivers without a header of its own keeps the sender’s headers on top, and a forged header there is read as the verdict. Check how your provider treats mail between two of its own customers before you rely on the gate.

:authserv-id takes one of:

  • a string, compared with the whole id, ignoring case: "mx.example.org";
  • a pattern, {:pattern "mx[0-9]+\\.example\\.org"}, matched against the whole id, ignoring case;
  • a list of both: ["mx.example.org" {:pattern "…"}].

A pattern always matches the whole id, so mx[0-9]+\.example\.org never accepts evil.mx1.example.org or mx1.example.org.attacker.test. It may use letters, digits and -, \. for a dot, \d, character classes such as [0-9], groups with alternatives such as (mx|smtp), and the quantifiers ?, *, + and {n,m}. It must end in a literal domain of at least two labels, such as \.example\.org. An unescaped ., ^, $, a top-level |, inline flags and any other construct are refused when the config loads, and so is a pattern that matches an empty id.

Some providers stamp the name of the receiving MX host rather than one id for the domain. Migadu stamps mx13.migadu.com or a sibling host, whichever received the message, so pin it with a pattern:

{:dkim {:require true :authserv-id {:pattern "mx[0-9]+\\.migadu\\.com"}}}

Migadu was seen adding no Authentication-Results header to mail sent from one Migadu mailbox to another, so such mail is refused. If Migadu also keeps an Authentication-Results header that a Migadu-hosted sender wrote into such a mail, that forged header is the topmost one; whether it does has not been checked.

Every IMAP and POP3 connection checks that the server’s certificate is trusted and names the host, and plaintext (:tls false) is refused for any host that is not written as a loopback address (localhost, 127.x.x.x, ::1).

Under systemd

One unit replaces the board’s service and every bridge timer. The keys of the delegates arrive as credentials; the store keys come from a password manager here, and {:credential …} works for them as well:

# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik-backend.service
[Unit]
Description=tik: the boards, MCP, bridges, mailboxes and notifier of every local store
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/tik backend --config %h/.config/tik/backend.edn
LoadCredential=github-work-key:%h/.config/tik/github-work_ed25519
LoadCredential=redmine-work-key:%h/.config/tik/redmine-work_ed25519
LoadCredential=mail-work-key:%h/.config/tik/mail-work_ed25519
LoadCredential=support-app-imap:%h/.config/tik/support-app-imap
# the MCP tokens live here; the backend refuses a token others can read
StateDirectory=tik-backend
StateDirectoryMode=0700
# tik exits with 143 on the SIGTERM of a stop, which is no failure.
SuccessExitStatus=143
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
# a stop also ends every run the backend started
KillMode=control-group

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

The backend refuses TIK_ROOT and the bridges’ token variables, so the unit sets none of them. Disable the bridge timers and the old board service when it starts, and point MCP clients at /s/<store>/mcp.

Reporter pseudonyms and block lists

A mailbox can record who sent each report without writing the address into the store, and refuse senders who only send garbage. Both keys go on a mailbox or at the top level as a default for all of them:

{:reporter {:key {:credential "reporter-key"}
            :table "~/.local/state/tik/reporters"
            :fact [:reporter :id]}
 :block {:addresses ["noise@example.net"]
         :domains ["spam.example"]
         :pseudonyms ["hmac-sha256:<64 hex digits>"]}}

With :reporter, a new ticket from a sender the DKIM gate authenticated carries the fact [:reporter :id] (or the :fact you name) holding hmac-sha256: and the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the lower-cased address under your key. Without the key nobody can reverse it; with it, a guessed address can be checked, so guard the key like a signing key. It comes from {:command …}, {:credential …} or {:file …}, holds at least 32 bytes (openssl rand -hex 32 prints 64), and is resolved once when the bridge starts. The bridge refuses to start when :reporter lacks a key, lacks :dkim {:require true …}, puts its table inside the store, or names a process that does not declare the fact with a schema a pseudonym satisfies:

:process/facts {[:reporter :id] [:re "^hmac-sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$"]}

A comment on an existing ticket records no pseudonym, and a tik> line in a mail can never set the reporter fact.

The table maps each pseudonym to its address and the time it was first seen. It is a directory only you can enter (0700), one file per pseudonym (0600), and it stays on this machine, outside the store, so it is never committed or pushed:

  • tik reporter show <pseudonym> resolves one;
  • tik reporter forget <address|pseudonym> deletes its rows for an erasure request, after which the pseudonym on the tickets resolves to nothing (backups of the table keep what they hold until they expire);
  • tik reporter stats [--format json] counts tickets per pseudonym, showing the address where a row exists and (forgotten) where none does.

Each takes --table <dir>, or reads the table from --config <imap.edn> (by default imap.edn, else bridge.edn, at the store’s root) with --mailbox <id> when the config names several.

:block refuses a sender after the DKIM gate and before anything is written; the poll logs the rule that matched, never the address or the body, and goes on with the next message. A domain matches itself and every subdomain on a label boundary, so spam.example also blocks mail.spam.example and not nospam.example. Listing :pseudonyms keeps plaintext out of the config and needs :reporter, whose key computes a sender’s pseudonym; a block by pseudonym still holds after the sender’s row was forgotten.

Hints

tik notify --config ~/.config/tik/notify.edn          # the notifier
tik notify watch --store work --where "stage=:asked"  # one JSON line per hint

See Claude Code for the notifier’s config and what a hint holds.

entry.title: MCP server
entry.content:
The frontier as an agent’s gated tool surface, and tik’s agent skill, over stdio or HTTP.
TIK_ACTOR=bot TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/bot_ed25519 tik mcp

tik mcp speaks the Model Context Protocol over stdio and exposes one store as a tool surface. The tools an agent is offered are exactly the steps the frontier admits for its role at that moment, so the tool list is the authorization boundary.

One shared server over HTTP

TIK_ACTOR=bot TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/bot_ed25519 \
  tik serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7777 --mcp-token-file ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token

tik serve also speaks MCP on /mcp when given a token file, so every client shares one long-running server instead of starting its own process. It answers one JSON-RPC message per POST with JSON and opens no event stream. A request needs the token as Authorization: Bearer …, and one whose Origin is not the server’s own is refused, which keeps a web page from driving the server through DNS rebinding. The token must be at least 32 characters; openssl rand -hex 32 makes one.

Without --host, a server offering MCP listens on 127.0.0.1 only, because /mcp writes over plain HTTP; put a TLS proxy in front before offering it beyond the machine. The board alone keeps listening on every address.

--surfaces picks what the server offers: http for the read-only board and its EDN, mcp for the tools, or http,mcp. Without it, the server offers http, and mcp too when a token file is given.

Agent skill

The server serves tik’s agent skill, the repository’s skills/tik/ tree as built into the binary, through the MCP Skills extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills):

  • skills/list and skills/get return the skill’s entry: its frontmatter and a manifest listing every file with its sha256 digest and size.
  • resources/read serves the files under skill://tik/<path>. A client without the extension sees them as ordinary resources, and the server instructions name skill://tik/SKILL.md.
  • A URI with a .. or . segment, an empty segment or an escaped character is refused, as is a skill name other than lowercase letters, digits and single inner hyphens, and any file the manifest does not list.

The extension’s digests only show that a file matches the manifest, and whoever runs the server writes both. tik therefore signs the manifest with TIK_KEY as TIK_ACTOR, in the SSHSIG namespace tik-skill-manifest, and puts the signature in the entry’s _meta under wtf.metio/skill-manifest. Without a key, that marker says "signed": false and why. tik skill verify checks a server against the store’s actors file:

tik skill verify http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp --token-file ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token

It checks the signature, then reads every file and compares its bytes, and the SKILL.md frontmatter, with the manifest. It exits 1 for an unsigned manifest, a signature no registered actor made, or any file that differs. Given a saved skills/list or skills/get response instead of a URL, it checks the signature alone. It accepts signatures in the namespaces tik-skill-manifest and kajero-skill-manifest, and a manifest that lists more than 512 files, declares a skill over 16 MiB, names an entry URI other than the skill’s SKILL.md or lists a file of another skill is malformed.

The signed bytes are the manifest in a fixed form, one line each: skill-manifest v1, skill <SKILL.md URI>, then file <digest> <size> <URI> per file in URI order, each line ending in a newline. The form leaves out the frontmatter, which a client compares against the signed SKILL.md bytes, and binds no server version, so an older signed manifest still verifies until its signer is removed from actors.

The server speaks both MCP eras: the initialize handshake of revisions up to 2025-06-18, and revision 2026-07-28, whose every request carries its version and capabilities in _meta. Claude Code lists a server’s skills only over 2026-07-28. Over HTTP, a 2026-07-28 request must repeat its version, method and resource or tool name in the MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, and is refused with 400 when they differ from the body.

A message is one JSON object of at most 1 MiB, read strictly: a key named twice, text after the value or a body over the limit answers a parse error (-32700) whose data.rule names the rule, without quoting the input. A request without "jsonrpc": "2.0", a string method and a string or integer id answers -32600, an unknown method -32601, and an unknown tool or arguments that are not an object -32602. A tool that runs and fails, such as a refused assertion or a missing argument, answers in its result with isError. A notification, a message without an id, runs nothing and gets no answer (202 over HTTP). Over stdio, a line over the limit is refused without being held in memory, and the next line is read as usual.

Why the boundary holds

An agent’s permission to act is derived from the same guards a person’s is. A step whose :signed-by names a role the agent is not in never appears as an available tool, and calling it anyway is refused with the derived reason rather than a generic denial.

That matters because the alternative — telling a model in its prompt what it may not do — is enforcement by cooperation. Here the check happens where the answer is computed, and it produces the same reason string a person would see.

Accountability

Every write the agent makes is an ordinary signed event with the agent’s own actor identity. The log therefore distinguishes what a person claimed from what an agent claimed, permanently and without a separate audit trail. tik causal names the events behind each reached stage, so a conclusion an agent contributed to can be traced to the evidence it supplied and the key that signed it.

Task specifications from guards

An agent asking “what should I do?” gets the same structured answer every other lens renders:

tik explain 3184 --actor bot --edn

Each missing step carries its path, its schema, and who may satisfy it — which makes an acceptance criterion out of a guard, rather than out of a sentence somebody wrote in a ticket description.

entry.title: Odoo
entry.content:
Odoo project tasks mirrored as odoo-task tickets, with their history.
tik bridge odoo --config odoo.edn                               # poll once
tik bridge odoo describe --model project.task --config odoo.edn # read a model's fields

tik bridge odoo mirrors Odoo project tasks into the store as tickets under the odoo-task process. Each ticket carries the task’s title, stage, assignee and project as facts signed by the bridge, its conversation as artifacts, and its URL as odoo.url. The stage follows the mirrored Odoo stage: :closed when the configuration names that stage as closed, :open for every other stage. Moving the task back to an open stage in Odoo brings the ticket back to :open on the next sync.

Odoo stays the place where the task is worked on. Facts you add locally (a link.* to another ticket, notes for yourself) stay in tik and never move the mirrored stages.

Configuration

{:profile       "project.task"             ; optional; the Odoo model to mirror
 :url           "https://odoo.example"
 :db            "odoo"                     ; the database name
 :user          "you@example.com"          ; a string or a secret spec
 :password      {:env "ODOO_PASSWORD"}     ; a secret spec
 :closed-stages ["Done" "Cancelled"]       ; stage names that count as closed
 :users         {45 "seb"}                 ; Odoo user id -> tik actor
 :domain        [["user_id" "=" 45]]       ; optional; default: tasks assigned to :user
 :actor         "odoo"
 :process       :odoo-task}

The bridge talks to Odoo’s JSON-RPC endpoint, /jsonrpc. Odoo 12 has no API keys, so it logs in with the user’s password and sends it with every call; a user with read access to the tasks is enough. Odoo often refuses to list its databases, in which case the database name shows after logging in through the web interface (/web/session/get_session_info reports it as db).

Odoo 12 stages carry no closed flag. Folding a stage only hides its column, and a folded backlog is still open work, so :closed-stages names the closed stages explicitly.

Each sweep syncs every task the domain selects, plus every task the store already mirrors, so a task that is reassigned or archived keeps its ticket current. A task counts as mirrored when the store holds its own ticket, the one whose id the host of :url, the model and odoo.id name; odoo.url plays no part, so changing the scheme, port or path of :url on the same host keeps every task, and a ticket of another host or model is never taken for one. :users renders an Odoo user as a tik actor in odoo.assignee; other users appear under the name Odoo shows.

Profiles

A profile describes how one Odoo model becomes tickets: which tracked fields become which facts, which field derives the ticket’s state and from which configuration lists, how the ticket title is formed, which chatter messages become artifacts, the default domain and the process. :profile names the profile by its model, as a string or a keyword, and defaults to "project.task". A configuration that names a model without a profile is refused when it loads, with the list of profiles there are.

Profile Facts State Title Configuration
project.task odoo.title, odoo.stage, odoo.assignee, odoo.project odoo.state: :closed for a stage in :closed-stages, else :open #<id> <title the task was created with> :closed-stages

Every profile also asserts odoo.id and odoo.url, whose URL names the model. The ticket id is a name-based UUID over the Odoo host, the model and the record id, so records of two models with the same id become two tickets.

Describing a model

tik bridge odoo describe --model helpdesk.ticket --config odoo.edn
tik bridge odoo describe --model project.task --edn
tik bridge odoo describe --model project.task --format json

tik bridge odoo describe asks the server how it defines one model’s fields and prints, for each field, its type, label, whether it is required or read-only, the model a relation points at, the values of a selection, and whether Odoo tracks it. Only tracked fields can be mirrored with their history, so this is the list to read before writing a profile for a new model. The output also says whether the model inherits mail.thread.

The command writes nothing to Odoo or to the store. It logs in and calls version, login and fields_get, and refuses every other call before it leaves tik, so a write method cannot be reached from it. It reads :url, :db, :user and :password from the same odoo.edn as the bridge; :password has to be a secret spec such as {:env "ODOO_PASSWORD"} or {:command "pasejo secret show …"}, and a literal password in the file is refused. Neither the output nor an error message carries the password.

Odoo 12 reports the tracking flag as track_visibility, later versions as tracking; the command asks for both and names the one the server answered with. When the server reports neither, every field’s tracked flag reads unknown. Whether message_post accepts a message_id argument also reads unknown: fields_get describes fields, and Odoo offers no read-only call that reports a method’s arguments.

When the model has a profile, the output ends with how the profile fits the server: the fields it reads that the server lacks, fields whose type differs from the one the profile declares, actor fields that do not point at res.users, mirrored fields the server does not track, and, for a state read from a selection field, the selection values no configuration list names, which fall to the profile’s default state. A stage field such as stage_id is a relation, so its stage names are records that fields_get cannot list.

History

Every event is a function of the task and its chatter. Odoo records each change of a tracked field as a tracking value in the chatter, with the old and new value as Odoo displays them. The ticket is dated by the task’s creation and carries the values the task was created with, recovered by undoing each tracked change from the current values. Each message then adds its changes at its own time, and a comment or email as an odoo/message/<id> artifact. A re-sync adds only the messages that are new, and two machines syncing the same Odoo write identical events.

Only the title, stage, assignee and project are mirrored, because those are the fields Odoo tracks. A tracking value names its field by the label the field had at the time, in the language of whoever made the change; the bridge reads every field’s label in every installed language and leaves out a label two fields share.

Open work

tik ls --all --where 'stage=:open and fact:odoo.assignee=seb'
tik stats --by odoo.project --until :closed

entry.title: Redmine
entry.content:
Redmine issues mirrored as redmine-issue tickets, with their history.
tik bridge redmine --config redmine.edn   # poll once

tik bridge redmine mirrors Redmine issues into the store as tickets under the redmine-issue process. Each ticket carries the issue’s status, assignee, priority, tracker, project, subject and due date as facts signed by the bridge, its description and notes as artifacts, and its URL as redmine.url. The stage follows the mirrored status: :open, or :closed when Redmine counts the status as closed. Reopening the issue in Redmine brings the ticket back to :open on the next sync.

Redmine stays the place where the issue is worked on. Facts you add locally (a link.* to another ticket, notes for yourself) stay in tik and never move the mirrored stages.

Configuration

{:url     "https://redmine.example"
 :key     {:env "REDMINE_API_KEY"}         ; your API key (My account → API access key)
 :query   {:assigned_to_id "me"}           ; issues.json filters; all statuses are included
 :users   {11 "seb"}                       ; Redmine user id -> tik actor
 :actor   "redmine"
 :process :redmine-issue}

Each sweep syncs every issue the query selects, plus every issue the store already mirrors, so an issue that is reassigned or moved keeps its ticket current. :users renders a Redmine user as a tik actor in redmine.assignee; other users appear under the name Redmine shows.

History

Every event is a function of the issue and its journal. The ticket is dated by the issue’s creation and carries the values the issue was opened with, recovered by undoing each journal entry from the current values. Each journal entry then adds its changes at its own time, and its note as a redmine/journal/<id> artifact. A re-sync adds only the entries that are new, and two machines syncing the same Redmine write identical events.

Statuses, priorities and trackers are rendered by name from Redmine’s current configuration. Renaming one in Redmine adds assertions under the new name on the next sync; the latest journal entry still decides the current value.

Open work

tik ls --all --where 'stage=:open and fact:redmine.assignee=seb'
tik stats --by redmine.project --until :closed
